Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend who has just started assembling furniture asks for a quick video call because the instructions are confusing.
Situation2: They are expected to deep clean every room, ensuring all areas are thoroughly sanitized.
Story:
I was halfway through scrubbing the bathroom tiles, sweat beading on my forehead, when my phone buzzed. It was Mia, my best friend, her name lighting up the screen with a desperate text: “Can you hop on a quick video call? I’m losing my mind with this bookshelf.” I knew she’d just moved in and was struggling to make her new place feel like home. As her friend, I wanted to be there, to help her through this little crisis, to laugh with her about the confusing instructions and celebrate when the last screw went in.

But the smell of bleach reminded me of my other role. My supervisor had been clear: every corner needed to be spotless, every surface sanitized. I was already behind schedule, and if I didn’t finish the deep clean, I’d risk a complaint or worse, my job. My hands trembled as I stared at the phone, torn between the urge to support Mia and the pressure to meet the high standards expected of me at work. The weight of both roles pressed down, and I felt caught in the middle, unable to move.
